subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Sputnik and the Dawn of the Space Age
description: Learn Sputnik and the Dawn of the Space Age in one minute.

hook.text: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik. It was the first artificial satellite—and it terrified the West.

buildup.text: Sputnik was a polished metal sphere just 58 cm across. It orbited Earth every 96 minutes, beeping on radio frequencies.

discovery.text: Anyone with a radio could hear it. The beeping proved that space was reachable—and the Soviets got there first.

twist.text: Sputnik's batteries died after 21 days. It burned up on reentry in January 1958. But it had already changed the world.

climax.text: The US created NASA in 1958 in direct response. The space race—and the modern space age—had begun.

punchline.text: A beeping metal ball. Twenty-one days in orbit. The space age began.

quiz.question: What was the immediate consequence of Sputnik's launch for the United States?
options: The creation of NASA and the start of the Space Race
The first crewed mission to the Moon
The development of the first space telescope

details.summary: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 on October 4, 1957 — the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth. This 58-centimeter, 84-kilogram sphere with radio antennas orbited for three months, beeping a signal heard worldwide. It triggered the Space Race and marked the beginning of the Space Age.
details.whyItMatters: Sputnik proved that leaving Earth was possible and sparked the Space Race that led to the Moon landings, space stations, and the entire modern space industry. It transformed astronomy from a purely observational science to an exploratory one.
takeaways: Sputnik 1 was the first artificial satellite, launched in 1957
It triggered the US-Soviet Space Race
It marks the beginning of the Space Age and space exploration

faq.question: Why did Sputnik cause panic in the West?
faq.answer: If the Soviets could launch a satellite, they could launch nuclear warheads anywhere on Earth via intercontinental ballistic missiles. Sputnik demonstrated a capability that threatened US military security. The US created NASA in 1958 and dramatically increased science education funding in response.

faq.question: What did Sputnik actually do in orbit?
faq.answer: It transmitted a simple radio 'beep' on two frequencies for 21 days until its batteries died. Scientists used the signal to study the ionosphere and the drag on its orbit to measure upper atmospheric density. It burned up on re-entry on January 4, 1958, after 1,440 orbits.
